{{Politics of Canada}}

Canada holds general elections, colloquially referred to as federal elections since the 1940s (and as dominion elections from 1867 to the 1940s), for the purpose of determining the political leadership of its national government, the [[Government of Canada]] (or the "federal government"), through [[Democracy|democratic]] means. The last [[general election]] was [[2025 Canadian federal election|held in April 2025]], through which the incumbent [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal]] government led by new party leader [[Mark Carney]] was re-elected with a [[Minority governments in Canada|minority mandate]].

This article provides a summary of results for [[Elections in Canada|Canadian general elections]] that has taken place since the nation was formed (via [[Canadian Confederation|confederation]]) in 1867. Upon the call of such a general election, all seats in the Canadian [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]] are vacated and contested in local elections to determine its new representative known as a [[Member of Parliament (Canada)|member of Parliament]] (MP). As of the election held in 2025, there are 343 MPs in Canada.

== Electoral system ==
Like other [[Westminster System|Westminster-style]] [[Parliamentary government|parliamentary governments]], Canadian voters exercise their democratic franchise indirectly by electing local representatives, known as members of Parliament (MPs), to the [[House of Commons of Canada|House of Commons]], the lower house of the [[Parliament of Canada]], via plurality voting (or the [[First-past-the-post voting|first-past-the-post system]]). All Canadian citizens age eighteen or above are entitled to vote in elections held for the [[Electoral district (Canada)|electoral district]] they reside in. The head of the Canadian federal government, the [[Prime Minister of Canada|prime minister of Canada]], is typically the MP that leads the political party with the most seats in the House of Commons. They are normally chosen by virtue of being the leader of the political party with a majority of the seats in the legislature or having secured the needed support from other parties to [[Confidence and supply|command the confidence]] of Parliament.

Since 1929, Canadian federal elections have been held on Mondays, or on Tuesdays immediately after a Monday that is a [[Statutory Holidays in Canada|statutory holiday]]. Section 4 of the [[Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms|Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedom]] requires that a general election be held no later than five years after the previous election. Since the end of [[World War II]], elections are usually held every three or four years. Under the [[Fixed election dates in Canada|fixed-date provisions]] of the ''[[Canada Elections Act]]'', a federal election must be held on the third Monday in October in the fourth calendar year after the polling day of the previous election.<ref name="C16">{{cite web |date=May 3, 2007|title=An Act to amend the Canada Elections Act|url=https://www.parl.ca/documentviewer/en/39-1/bill/C-16/royal-assent/page-27?col=2|url-status=live|archive-url=https://www.parl.ca/Content/Bills/391/Government/C-16/C-16_4/C-16_4.PDF|archive-date=June 25, 2024|archive-format=PDF|access-date=June 25, 2024|publisher=LegisINFO|format=}}</ref> However, the election may occur before that date if the [[Governor General of Canada|governor general]] dissolves Parliament on the recommendation of the prime minister, either for a [[List of snap elections in Canada|snap election]] or after Parliament expresses its lack of confidence through the rejection of a [[Loss of supply|supply bill]] (which last occurred [[1980 Canadian federal election|in 1979]]) or the adoption of a [[motion of no confidence]] (which last occurred [[2011 Canadian federal election|in 2011]]).

Since 1920, all elections held for the purpose of electing MPs have been administered by the [[Chief Electoral Officer of Canada|chief electoral officer]], who heads the independent agency [[Elections Canada]] and is accountable to Parliament rather than to the government in power. Election finances has been regulated since the 1970s, and that function was separated from Elections Canada and transferred to the [[commissioner of Canada Elections]] in 1977.

== Electoral dynamics ==
Two political parties, the [[Liberal Party of Canada|Liberal Party]] and the [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservative Party]], have been the principal contenders for power in the 21st century. The same two parties{{Spaced en dash}}in the Conservative Party's case, along with its various previous incarnations and factions{{Spaced en dash}}have dominated [[Politics of Canada|politics in Canada]] by alternating governing between them to the exclusion of all other parties at the national level. Since 1921, however, the two main parties had to contend with other forces occasionally displacing them from second place, most recently [[2011 Canadian federal election|in 2011]] when the [[New Democratic Party]] displaced the Liberals to become the largest opposition party in Parliament.

With only two exceptions, transitions of power between the parties have always occurred as the result of general elections. The exception were in 1873 and in 1926, when the respective incumbent Conservative and Liberal government were brought down by scandals. In 1873, the Liberals formed government and secured an electoral mandate through a general election within two months. In 1926, the Conservative Party took power but failed to win the subsequent election that took place three months later.

Since the nation was [[Canadian Confederation|formed in 1867]], Canada has held forty-five general elections. The Liberals won the most seats in twenty-six elections, in seventeen instances attaining a majority of the seats. Rival Conservatives won the most seats in nineteen elections (once under the [[Unionist Party (Canada)|Unionist]] banner), attaining a majority of the seats in thirteen instances. In one instance [[1925 Canadian federal election|in 1925]], the Conservatives won the most seats, but the incumbent Liberals remained in office with the support of the third-place [[Progressive Party of Canada|Progressive Party]]. In six elections, the largest party won the most seats and formed government despite having won a smaller share of the popular vote as their main rival. That was the case with the Progressive Conservative governments formed [[1957 Canadian federal election|in 1957]] and [[1979 Canadian federal election|in 1979]], and the Liberal governments formed following the elections [[1896 Canadian federal election|of 1896]], [[1926 Canadian federal election|1926]], [[2019 Canadian federal election|2019]] and [[2021 Canadian federal election|2021]].

In addition to the two main parties, there has been significant parliamentary presence of smaller parties since 1921 when the [[Progressive Party of Canada|Progressive Party]] (and its allied [[United Farmers of Canada|United Farmers movement]]) displaced the Conservatives as the largest opposition party. As the principal alternative to the two main party, the Progressive Party was supplanted by the [[Social Credit Party of Canada|Social Credit Party]] and the [[Co-operative Commonwealth Federation]] (CCF) in the 1930s, both formally entering Parliament [[1935 Canadian federal election|in 1935]], with the CCF and its official successor the [[New Democratic Party]] (NDP) having maintained a continual presence since, while the Social Credit Party ceased to be represented as of the [[1980 Canadian federal election|1980 election]].

The presence of smaller parties unsurprisingly led to occasional minority parliaments, which remained a rare event until the end of the [[World War II]]. Of the twenty elections that took place in Canada's first eight decades, only three resulted in minority parliaments. The subsequent ten elections resulted in five minority parliaments, all within a fifteen-year timespan between [[1957 Canadian federal election|the 1957]] and [[1972 Canadian federal election|1972 general elections]]. After two decades of mostly majority governments, minority parliaments become common at the start of 21st century. Six of the eight elections since 2000 have resulted in minority parliaments, including the most recent three elections.  

The [[Progressive Conservative Party of Canada|Progressive Conservative Party]] suffered the most dramatic defeat ever experienced by a sitting government in the [[1993 Canadian federal election|1993 election]] when it went from a majority government with 169 seats to a group without [[official party status]], having only won two seats. The downfall of the traditional Progressive Conservative Party in the 1990s was a result of discontent manifested in the populist [[Reform Party of Canada|Reform Party]] in [[western Canada]] and the separatist [[Bloc Québécois]] in [[Quebec]]. The Reform Party rebranded as the [[Canadian Alliance]] in 2000 before uniting with the Progressive Conservatives in 2003 to form the modern [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservative Party]], which formed government shortly after in 2006. The [[Green Party of Canada|Green Party]] secured it first seat in 2011, which it has held since, but has not since been able to expand its presence in a meaningful way.

== Other lists of Canadian elections ==

* [[List of federal by-elections in Canada|Federal by-elections]] – held in select electoral districts to fill vacancies midterms caused by death of resignation
* General elections are held in each province and territories to elect their respective provincial government. For a timeline of all provincial elections, see [[Timeline of Canadian elections]].
* [[List of elections in the Province of Canada|General elections in the Province of Canada]] – eight general elections were held between 1841 and 1864 in the [[Province of Canada]], the British colony that was the largest predecessor of Canada
* Elections have been held in what is now Canada since as early [[1st General Assembly of Nova Scotia|as 1758]], when the colony of Nova Scotia elected its first general assembly. Of the four original provinces:
** [[List of Nova Scotia General Assemblies#Pre-Confederation|Twenty-two general elections]] were held in Nova Scotia prior to Confederation
** [[General elections in New Brunswick (pre-Confederation)|Twenty-one general elections]] were held in New Brunswick prior to Confederation, beginning in 1785
** Thirteen general elections were held in Upper Canada (now part of [[Ontario]]) between 1792 and 1836 for the [[Legislative Assembly of Upper Canada]]
** Fifteen elections were held in Lower Canada (now part of [[Quebec]]) between 1792 and 1834 for the [[Legislative Assembly of Lower Canada]]

|{{efn-ur|name=e1993|[[Jean Chrétien]]'s Liberals win a majority, soundly defeating the Progressive Conservatives, led by new prime minister [[Kim Campbell]], who are left in fifth place with just two seats, their worst ever showing. The [[Bloc Québécois]], founded in 1990 and led by ex-Mulroney cabinet minister [[Lucien Bouchard]], becomes the Official Opposition. Reform becomes the third party. [[Audrey McLaughlin]]'s New Democrats also post their worst results to this point with just nine seats. The election marks the end of the predominantly three-party Liberal–Progressive Conservative–NDP system.}}

|{{efn-ur|name=e2025|Former [[Bank of Canada]] and [[Bank of England]] Governor [[Mark Carney]] led Liberals to minority victory while a first time candidate for any public office, the first person with no prior electoral experience to lead a party to victory. Conservatives led by [[Pierre Poilievre]] won over 40% share of popular vote, a new watermark for the modern Conservative Party, but failed to form government, the first time a party with more than 40% popular vote not forming government since 1979 when Liberal Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau with 40.1% was ousted by Progressive Conservative Joe Clark with 35.9%. NDP lost official party status for the first time since 1993 and its leader Jagmeet Singh was defeated locally.}}
